title: The stained cloth
hook: a dirty cloth won't take the dye; a cleansed mind takes the good (MN 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: fear and dread, and your line, face it where it finds you. When a small fear showed up, did you stay put for three breaths? Day four hundred seven.
screen: `FEAR AND DREAD — FACE IT WHERE IT FINDS YOU.`

segments.voice: Anyone who has ever dyed a T-shirt learns the rule the hard way. Wash it first. If there's grease or grime in the cotton, the color comes out patchy and dull, however good the dye is, and more dye won't fix it. You can't cover a stain with color. You have to take it out, and then the color holds. The Buddha used exactly this picture to talk about the mind. Today: the stained cloth.
screen: `WASH IT FIRST.` → `MORE DYE WON'T FIX IT.` → `THEN THE COLOR HOLDS.`

segments.voice: MN 7, the Vatthupama, the simile of the cloth. Suppose a cloth were stained and dirty, the Buddha says, and a dyer dipped it in blue, or yellow, or red, or crimson. It would come out badly dyed, impure in color. Why? Because the cloth wasn't clean. But dip a clean, bright cloth, and it takes the dye beautifully. In the same way, he says, when the mind is stained, an unhappy destination can be expected; when the mind is clean, a happy one. Then he names the stains, sixteen of them: covetousness, ill will, anger, revenge, contempt, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, rivalry, conceit, arrogance, vanity and negligence. It's an old list, and it could describe an ordinary week online. The key move is seeing a stain as a stain, and letting it go. Then the cloth is ready. And what color does it take? Confidence in the Buddha, the teaching and the community. Then the four immeasurables: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, filling the world in every direction. The order matters. Not dye first and hope it covers. Clean first; then the color holds. The Dhammapada has a dyed-cloth verse too, in Max Müller's translation: “He who wishes to put on the yellow dress without having cleansed himself from sin” is not worthy of it, the verse goes on. The robe is the color. The washing comes first.
screen: `A STAINED CLOTH TAKES DYE BADLY.` · `SIXTEEN STAINS OF THE MIND.` · `SEE THE STAIN, LET IT GO.` · `CLEAN FIRST, THEN THE COLOR HOLDS.` · then, large: `CLEAN CLOTH TAKES DYE.`

segments.voice: Pick one stain from the list that you recognize: envy, maybe, or an old grudge, or vanity. Don't scrub at it. Just see it plainly, the way you'd hold a shirt up to the light and say: there's the mark. On each out-breath, loosen your grip on it a little. Then, for the last part of the sit, let one color in: wish one person well. And after the bell, if you like, clean one real thing: a cup, a desk, a shirt. The bell holds the time.
The stained cloth. A dirty cloth won't take the dye; a mind washed of its stains takes the good.
Your line: clean cloth takes dye. Today, before you start something good, clear one small thing first: a grudge, a cluttered desk, an apology you owe. Day four hundred seven.

howItsDone: In Theravada and other monastic communities, robes are traditionally dyed in ochre, saffron or brown, and teachers often use the image of washing before dyeing to describe purifying the mind before cultivating the immeasurables.

with anger, contempt, stinginess, vanity and the rest.
in MN 7, the clean mind takes on the four immeasurables
loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, in every direction.

fork.setup: you're a dyer with a beautiful crimson dye and a stained, dirty cloth. what does the simile say happens when you dip it?
options: the color comes out patchy and impure
fork.reveal: it comes out badly dyed, because the cloth wasn't clean. the mind is the same: see the stains, let them go, and then the good takes.

original.note: Pali upakkilesa: defilement, stain; the sutta's word for the sixteen.

trapdoor: what you thought: be a good person and good things happen.
what it means: clear the mind's stains first, and then the good qualities take hold.
what a scholar hears: vattha is cloth, upakkilesa a stain or defilement; the sixteen run from covetousness to negligence, and the 'color' is confidence in the three jewels and the four immeasurables.

sources.quoted: He who wishes to put on the yellow dress without having cleansed himself from sin

notes: Dhammapada 9 opening quoted from Max Müller (1881) from memory; the rest of the verse is paraphrased. Please confirm.
The sixteen defilements are translated loosely (e.g. palasa as 'domineering', sarambha as 'rivalry'); please confirm the English choices.
The sutta's ending with the brahmin Sundarika Bharadvaja and the river is left out on purpose to keep the day on one idea.
